summary: A web tool that lets anyone explore real NASA SPHEREx infrared observations. Enter right ascension and declination or open one of six examples covering the five challenge targets. Play the sky through time, pan to nearby fields, compare dates, and inspect spectra with uncertainties and missing samples. Catalog overlays and position measurements help users distinguish known sources from changes worth investigating. Every image keeps its observation time and archive provenance. The viewer requests small cutouts as needed and keeps the examples playable during archive search outages.
details:
SPHEREx Sky Viewer turns a sky coordinate into a sequence of real infrared observations in a browser. Start with Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae or R Draconis. A sixth example uses the original WISE 0855 coordinates supplied by the challenge. Filter by date, detector or wavelength, then play, pause, step or scrub. The timeline groups observations by UTC date, week, month or survey pass and shows gaps between observations.

The viewer uses familiar map controls. Drag to explore nearby sky, scroll or pinch to zoom, or use the keyboard. The viewer shows the new coordinates separately and lets you return to your entered target. Panning loads small cutouts from known exposures after movement stops. Search archive here explicitly looks for other exposures. Shared links restore the chosen field and observations. The interface works on phones and explains the difference between faint sky and pixels that are missing or masked.

Compare dates side by side, blink between them, or use a sum or signed difference heatmap to see where brightness changed. Mark a feature in two images to measure its angular shift. When the data pass quality checks, the viewer can group changes into candidates, suggest catalog matches, rank candidates, and estimate a short future path with uncertainty. Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays help identify known objects. Their explanations work by hover, keyboard focus or touch. Downloadable measurements retain the original observation references.

Pick a sky position or source to plot infrared brightness against wavelength. The spectrum shows measured points, uncertainties, observation dates and gaps. An extended extraction can retrieve additional calibration. A separate DR1 all-sky cube view offers spectral context across 102 nominal channels. The tool also supports a matched-wavelength light curve and attempts to combine compatible exposures from the same visit.

We built the interface with TypeScript, Vite and Canvas and the API with Python and FastAPI. Astropy handles FITS files and sky coordinates. NumPy, SciPy and Pillow support alignment, measurements and rendering. Uvicorn and Caddy serve the app over HTTPS on a Linux server. Small cutouts, request limits and a cache that evicts older results keep it practical on one server. The bundled examples and a static fallback keep the core experience available during archive outages. The original software uses the MIT License.

Our goal is to make the Planet X challenge approachable through repeatable observation and comparison. Wavelength, coverage, masking and alignment checks help users judge whether a change merits follow-up. One measured spectrum agreed with IRSA’s reference within our stated tolerance. Controlled tests verified candidate recognition and a motion forecast against a held-out observation. Real-field candidate ranking and forecasting, and a successful combination of compatible real exposures from one visit, still need validation.
